questions.q: The Chief Editor says formal education “can give you a job, but it cannot teach you the art of living.” What, in his view, fills this gap?
options: Professional training on the job
Not quite. The article says: Informal education that instils spiritual and social values, such as a magazine can offer.
Longer years at university
Not quite. The article says: Informal education that instils spiritual and social values, such as a magazine can offer.
Informal education that instils spiritual and social values, such as a magazine can offer
Yes. That is the stated purpose of the magazine.
Travel to other countries
Not quite. The article says: Informal education that instils spiritual and social values, such as a magazine can offer.
questions.rationale: The editorial calls the magazine “an institution for informal education” whose purpose is “to promote spiritual values in society.”

questions.q: Why does the article say that four anti-corruption movements in India did not reach their goal?
options: They made demands of the system, whereas corruption begins in the individual mind
Exactly. The article asks for minds to be re-engineered, not systems.
They had no well-known leaders
Not quite. The article says: They made demands of the system, whereas corruption begins in the individual mind.
They did not draw large enough crowds
Not quite. The article says: They made demands of the system, whereas corruption begins in the individual mind.
The laws they asked for were never written
Not quite. The article says: They made demands of the system, whereas corruption begins in the individual mind.
questions.rationale: “It is not the system that is responsible for corruption; it is the human mind… Any movement that intends to achieve its goal must target individual minds, rather than the system.”

questions.q: “To shorten a line, you only need to draw a longer line next to it.” How does the article apply this image to corruption?
options: Punish small offences so that large ones look worse
Not quite. The article says: Give people a goal higher than money – wisdom and spiritual growth – and money loses its hold.
Shorten the time courts take to decide cases
Not quite. The article says: Give people a goal higher than money – wisdom and spiritual growth – and money loses its hold.
Give people a goal higher than money – wisdom and spiritual growth – and money loses its hold
Well done. Money becomes a need, not a goal.
Pay officials more than they could take in bribes
Not quite. The article says: Give people a goal higher than money – wisdom and spiritual growth – and money loses its hold.
questions.rationale: “We have to replace money as a goal with wisdom as a goal… to eradicate corruption, we have to give individuals a goal greater than money.”

questions.q: The article compares religion to nuclear energy. What is the point of the comparison?
options: Both were discovered by modern science
Not quite. The article says: Both are sources of life as given by nature and God; the harm comes from human misuse.
Both will one day be exhausted
Not quite. The article says: Both are sources of life as given by nature and God; the harm comes from human misuse.
Both are sources of life as given by nature and God; the harm comes from human misuse
Right. The fault lies with man, not with the gift.
Both are too dangerous for ordinary people
Not quite. The article says: Both are sources of life as given by nature and God; the harm comes from human misuse.
questions.rationale: “It is wrong to blame religion for the evils which men have perpetrated in its name. This is the fault of man, not the fault of the divine religion which he corrupts.”

questions.q: What lesson does the article draw from the life of Abd al-Rahman, the Umayyad prince who fled Damascus and later ruled al-Andalus?
options: It is wiser to stay hidden when enemies are strong
Not quite. The article says: When one opportunity ends another arises, but it must be seized with courage and perseverance.
Success depends on having a large army
Not quite. The article says: When one opportunity ends another arises, but it must be seized with courage and perseverance.
When one opportunity ends another arises, but it must be seized with courage and perseverance
Yes. He had nothing but “his own wits and perseverance.”
Noble birth always brings a person back to power
Not quite. The article says: When one opportunity ends another arises, but it must be seized with courage and perseverance.
questions.rationale: “There is no end to the opportunities in this world. When one opportunity ceases to exist, another opportunity always arises elsewhere… It takes a person of courage to grasp opportunities.”

questions.q: Which formula does the article offer for harmony among people of different religions?
options: Accept every religion as equally true
The article says this goes against each believer’s inner conviction and is not practical.
Merge the religions into one shared creed
Not quite. The article says: Follow one and respect all.
Follow one and respect all
Correct. Mutual respect is practical even where agreement is not.
Keep religion out of human life
The article says the urge to believe is part of human nature and cannot be removed.
questions.rationale: “Mutual recognition of religion might not be practical, but mutual respect certainly is… a formula for maintaining religious harmony is—follow one and respect all.”

questions.q: On what ground does the article call Stephen Hawking’s statement “There is no heaven” unscientific?
options: Hawking was not trained in religion
Not quite. The article says: Science can speak only of what is observable, and that is about 4% of the universe.
The statement was made in a newspaper, not a journal
Not quite. The article says: Science can speak only of what is observable, and that is about 4% of the universe.
Science can speak only of what is observable, and that is about 4% of the universe
Exactly. Nothing can be asserted by science about the rest.
Other physicists have observed heaven
Not quite. The article says: Science can speak only of what is observable, and that is about 4% of the universe.
questions.rationale: The article says the only valid statement would have been: “according to known physical laws, in the 4% of the Universe subject to scientific study, there is probably no heaven.”

questions.q: Writing about Japan’s recovery after the 2011 earthquake and tsunami, what does the article say about adversity?
options: It matters less than complacency only in rich countries
Not quite. The article says: It is not good in itself, but with the will to act it can bring out hidden potential.
It ruins nations that lack natural resources
Not quite. The article says: It is not good in itself, but with the will to act it can bring out hidden potential.
It is not good in itself, but with the will to act it can bring out hidden potential
Well read. The will is the deciding thing.
It is always a blessing and should be sought
Not quite. The article says: It is not good in itself, but with the will to act it can bring out hidden potential.
questions.rationale: “By no means does this imply that adversity is itself beneficial. It is not. But it can be the spark which ignites the fuel of our souls… But for all this, there has to be the will to do so.”

questions.q: The article notes that a mountain stream does not try to remove the stones in its path. What should we learn from it?
options: To go around obstacles and keep moving instead of colliding with them
Yes. The stream “carves its way ahead around and alongside the stones.”
To change our destination when the path is blocked
Not quite. The article says: To go around obstacles and keep moving instead of colliding with them.
To gather strength until obstacles can be broken
Not quite. The article says: To go around obstacles and keep moving instead of colliding with them.
To wait patiently until obstacles are removed by others
Not quite. The article says: To go around obstacles and keep moving instead of colliding with them.
questions.rationale: The stream is “as if telling us not to collide with obstacles, but to continue on our way by keeping away from them.”

questions.q: According to the article, how does man’s following of the “universal model” differ from that of the stars, plants and streams?
options: Nature follows it by compulsion; man has to adopt it consciously, of his own free will
Right. That is the test of human freedom.
Nature gives and takes, man is asked only to give
Not quite. The article says: Nature follows it by compulsion; man has to adopt it consciously, of his own free will.
Man may follow it in part, nature must follow it fully
Not quite. The article says: Nature follows it by compulsion; man has to adopt it consciously, of his own free will.
Man follows it only in worship, nature at all times
Not quite. The article says: Nature follows it by compulsion; man has to adopt it consciously, of his own free will.
questions.rationale: “In the rest of the Universe, the model has been established compulsively, under the laws of nature, while we have to establish this model in our lives consciously, of our own free will.”
